description: I am a solo participant and citizen scientist working on the Zooniverse Planet Hunters TESS project. My main focus is analyzing light curves and finding transits of exoplanets. For this NASA Space Apps Challenge, I have selected the "Planet X and SPHEREx" challenge to apply my data analysis skills and explore planetary discoveries.
summary: To solve the challenge of spotting moving objects among billions of static stars in massive sky surveys like SPHEREx and TESS, I developed 'Planet Hunter'—a mathematical angular velocity filtering framework built on human vigilance. Drawing from my experience of completing over 1,951 citizen science classifications on Zooniverse (@gitgu), this tool helps everyday explorers distinguish true moving celestial bodies from gravitational lensing events. As proof of concept on Zooniverse Subject 126063062, I tracked a bright object across TESS pixel arrays (21 arcseconds/pixel) from 17.65 to 17.99 days, calculating an angular velocity of ~700 arcseconds/day. Because this speed brackets Mars and Jupiter, it confirms a likely main-belt asteroid, offering a fast, scalable way to verify real space discoveries.
details: Planet Hunter' is a citizen-science mathematical filtering model designed to detect moving celestial bodies—such as main-belt asteroids—within massive astronomical sky surveys like TESS and SPHEREx. While automated pipelines can struggle to separate faint moving objects from billions of static background stars or transient gravitational lensing events, 'Planet Hunter' combines human visual vigilance with angular velocity kinematics. Step-by-Step Methodology & Proof of Concept (Subject 126063062): Drawing from my personal experience completing over 1,951 classifications across 16 Zooniverse projects (username: @gitgu), I analyzed Zooniverse Subject 126063062 using TESS pixel arrays (where each pixel spans 21 arcseconds). When a bright object appeared to cross the field of view, I recorded its exact entry timestamp (17.65 days) and exit timestamp (17.99 days). Applying the Pythagorean theorem across the pixel coordinate grid to find total angular displacement and dividing by the elapsed time (0.34 days), the object's angular velocity came out to roughly 700 arcseconds per day. Because this speed cleanly brackets the average apparent velocities of Mars and Jupiter, it confirms the discovery is a physical moving body—specifically a likely main-belt asteroid—rather than a stationary gravitational lensing event. Benefits & Intended Impact: This framework empowers everyday citizen scientists to quickly verify moving objects without needing supercomputers. It reduces false positives in massive datasets and accelerates the discovery and tracking of near-Earth and main-belt asteroids. Tools & Resources Used: Zooniverse Citizen Science Platform (@gitgu), NASA TESS (Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite) pixel data, SPHEREx mission framework, Euclidean/Pythagorean coordinate geometry, and angular kinematics. Creativity & Key Factors Considered: Instead of relying purely on black-box AI, this project creatively turns human pattern recognition into a quantitative verification tool. Key factors considered include pixel scale resolution (21 arcseconds/pixel), entry/exit timing precision, and comparative planetary orbital speeds to rule out background noise and lensing artifacts
